title: An open singleton-fibre neighbourhood at a zero-dimensional closed fibre point
statement: Let $g:Y\to S$ be a morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme] locally of finite presentation [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. Let $s\in S$, let $y$ be a closed point [def-weil-closed-points] of the scheme-theoretic fibre $Y_s$ [def-pc-scheme-fibre], and suppose $\dim\mathcal O_{Y_s,y}=0$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. There is an open subscheme $j:V\hookrightarrow Y$ [def-weil-open-immersion] containing the image of $y$, such that the fibre $V_s$ has exactly one point $v$, the induced map $V_s\to Y_s$ sends $v$ to $y$, and $g\circ j$ is locally quasi-finite [pqf-def-quasifinite] and locally of finite presentation. If $g$ is flat [def-weil-flat-morphism], then $g\circ j$ is flat as well.

source.place: Tag 0570, label lemma-slice-CM, proof, case d=0: the open quasi-finite singleton-fibre neighbourhood; use local-ring dimension via Tag 00OU, algebra-lemma-dimension-closed-point-finite-type-field.

proof.text: Write $x$ for the image of $y$ in $Y$, so $g(x)=s$. First $g$ is locally of finite type. Indeed, for any affine open $T\subseteq S$, cover $g^{-1}(T)$ by affine opens $H$ using the affine-open basis. The affine finite-presentation criterion gives a presentation of $\mathcal O_Y(H)$ over $\mathcal O_S(T)$ with finitely many generators and relations. Forgetting the relations shows that it is a finitely generated algebra. This affine cover is exactly the locally finite type condition.

Choose affine neighbourhoods $W=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq Y$ of $x$ and $T=\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq S$ of $s$, with $g(W)\subseteq T$ and $A$ finitely presented over $R$, as allowed by local finite presentation. Let $\mathfrak q\subset A$ and $\mathfrak p\subset R$ represent $x$ and $s$, respectively, and put $k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ and $F=k\otimes_R A$. The affine-fibre-point lemma gives an open immersion $\operatorname{Spec}F\to Y_s$ onto the inverse image of $W$, and identifies $y$ with a prime $\mathfrak Q\subset F$ contracting to $\mathfrak q$. It also gives that $F$ is a finite type $k$-algebra. Its hypotheses require only the finite presentation just chosen, not flatness.

source.place: Tags 01JR, lemma-open-fibre-product, and 01JQ, lemma-fibre-product-affines, in the affine-fibre construction used for Tag 0570, lemma-slice-CM, d=0.

proof.text: The point $\mathfrak Q$ is closed in $\operatorname{Spec}F$, since $y$ is closed in $Y_s$ and the chart is an open subspace. Thus $\mathfrak Q$ is maximal: the closure of a prime $\mathfrak Q$ in the Zariski topology is the set of primes containing it, so a proper ideal strictly containing $\mathfrak Q$ would be contained in a maximal prime giving another point of that closure. The affine-open stalk-localization theorem applied to this chart identifies $F_{\mathfrak Q}$ with $\mathcal O_{Y_s,y}$. A ring isomorphism identifies prime ideals and their strict inclusions, hence preserves ring Krull dimension, so $\dim F_{\mathfrak Q}=0$. Apply the closed-point dimension theorem over the field $k$ to the finite type algebra $F$ and its maximal ideal $\mathfrak Q$: it gives $\dim_{\mathfrak Q}\operatorname{Spec}F=\dim F_{\mathfrak Q}=0$.

source.place: Tag 00OU, lemma-dimension-closed-point-finite-type-field; stalk identification: schemes.tex Tag 01HV, lemma-spec-sheaves, and Tag 01HF, example-open-subspace.

proof.text: Use the algebra tensor universal property to form the maps $F\to F'=A\otimes_Rk$, $\lambda\otimes a\mapsto a\otimes\lambda$, and $F'\to F$, $a\otimes\lambda\mapsto\lambda\otimes a$. Both composites fix the two factor inclusions, so uniqueness in that property makes them identities. Contravariant functoriality of the affine spectrum sends these inverse ring maps to inverse scheme morphisms, hence to a homeomorphism of spectra. If $\sigma:F\to F'$ is the swap, the corresponding prime in $F'$ is $\sigma(\mathfrak Q)$; its inverse image under $A\to F'$, $a\mapsto a\otimes1$, is $\mathfrak q$, since $\sigma^{-1}(a\otimes1)=1\otimes a$. It is therefore the unique fibre prime $\overline{\mathfrak q}$ over $\mathfrak q$ in the ring criterion. Let $h:\operatorname{Spec}F\to\operatorname{Spec}F'$ be the homeomorphism sending $\mathfrak Q$ to $\overline{\mathfrak q}$. The mutually inverse operations $N\mapsto h(N)$ and $N'\mapsto h^{-1}(N')$ give a bijection between their open neighbourhoods. On each pair $N,h(N)$ the restricted homeomorphism gives $\dim N=\dim h(N)$ by homeomorphism invariance of Krull dimension. Thus the two sets of neighbourhood dimensions agree; their minima, defining point dimension, agree as well, giving $\dim_{\overline{\mathfrak q}}\operatorname{Spec}F'=0$. The ring quasi-finiteness/zero-fibre-dimension criterion applies to $R\to A$, which is finite type by its finite presentation. It makes $R\to A$ quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$. The pair $W,T$ is therefore a witness that $g$ is quasi-finite at $x$ by the scheme definition.

source.place: Tag 0397, lemma-locally-quasi-finite-rel-dimension-0, affine specialization; Tag 01TD, definition-quasi-finite; tensor convention from schemes.tex Tag 01I4, lemma-fibre-product-affine-schemes.

proof.text: The quasi-finite-points-open theorem gives an open $U\subseteq Y$ containing $x$ with $g|_U$ locally quasi-finite. Since $g$ is locally of finite type (step 1) and quasi-finite at $x$ (step 4), the isolated-fibre-point theorem gives that $\{y\}$ is open in $Y_s$. By the fibre-topology statement the projection $Y_s\to Y$ is a homeomorphism onto the subspace $g^{-1}(s)$. Thus $\{x\}$ is open in $g^{-1}(s)$. By the definition of subspace topology there is an open $O\subseteq Y$ with $O\cap g^{-1}(s)=\{x\}$. Set $V=O\cap U$, as an open subscheme of $Y$. Since $x\in O\cap U$, it lies in $V$. Conversely, any $z\in V\cap g^{-1}(s)$ lies in $O\cap g^{-1}(s)=\{x\}$, so $z=x$. Thus $V\cap g^{-1}(s)=\{x\}$.

source.place: Tag 0570, lemma-slice-CM, proof d=0; morphisms.tex Tags 01TI, lemma-quasi-finite-points-open, and 01TH, lemma-quasi-finite-at-point-characterize; schemes.tex Tag 01K1, lemma-fibre-topological.

proof.text: Let $j:V\hookrightarrow Y$ be the open inclusion. Apply restriction of a locally quasi-finite morphism to $g|_U$, with source open $V\subseteq U$ and target open all of $S$; it gives that $g\circ j$ is locally quasi-finite. The fibre-topology statement for $g\circ j$ identifies $|V_s|$ with $V\cap g^{-1}(s)=\{x\}$, so $V_s$ has exactly one point $v$. Write $p_V:V_s\to V$ and $r_V:V_s\to\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)$ for its projections. The maps $j\circ p_V$ and $r_V$ have equal composites to $S$, by the defining fibre square for $g\circ j$. Thus the fibre-product universal property defining $Y_s$ gives the induced map $h:V_s\to Y_s$ with $p_Y\circ h=j\circ p_V$, where $p_Y:Y_s\to Y$ is the first projection. Consequently $p_Y(h(v))=x=p_Y(y)$. The fibre-topology statement makes $p_Y$ injective, so $h(v)=y$.

source.place: Tag 01TH, lemma-quasi-finite-at-point-characterize, (4), local nature of local quasi-finiteness; schemes.tex Tag 01K1, lemma-fibre-topological.

proof.text: For any $z\in V$, choose an affine open $T_z\subseteq S$ containing $g(z)$ and an affine open $H_z\subseteq V\cap g^{-1}(T_z)$ containing $z$, using the affine-open basis. Since $V$ is open in $Y$ with restricted structure sheaf, $H_z$ is also an affine open of $Y$. The affine finite-presentation criterion for $g$ makes $\mathcal O_S(T_z)\to\mathcal O_Y(H_z)=\mathcal O_V(H_z)$ finitely presented. The section map for $g\circ j$ on this pair of charts is the same ring map: $j$ restricts sections to $H_z$, and $\mathcal O_V(H_z)=\mathcal O_Y(H_z)$ with identical restrictions. These charts therefore witness that $g\circ j$ is locally of finite presentation. Finally, if $g$ is flat, the neighbourhoods of $z$ contained in $V$ are cofinal among its neighbourhoods in $Y$: intersect any neighbourhood with $V$. On those opens the structure sheaves and their restriction maps agree, so their stalk colimits identify $\mathcal O_{V,z}$ with $\mathcal O_{Y,z}$ and identify the structural maps from $\mathcal O_{S,g(z)}$. Their flatness is therefore the same, giving flatness of $g\circ j$ at every $z\in V$.
